extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democratic institutions, press freedom, and political associations
extracted.subtask_short: liberty of the press and associations
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles and practical criteria for assessing freedom of the press and the right of political association in democratic societies, including when repression or limitation may be (im)practicable, structural factors affecting influence, and dangers/benefits of associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No tenable middle ground between total press independence and total subjection
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one could point out an intermediate and yet a tenable position between the complete independence and the entire subjection of the public expression of opinion, I should perhaps be inclined to adopt it; but the difficulty is to discover this position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to prosecute or partially restrain the press tend to either publicize the censured ideas (via trials, pleadings) or drive suppression farther (requiring censorship of speech as well). Thus partial measures often fail: too much and too little has been tried; establishing censorship tends toward despotism because speech will find other outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as necessary guarantee where ordinary tribunals cannot restrain officials
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain countries ... every individual agent of the Government may violate the laws with impunity, since those whom he oppresses cannot prosecute him before the courts of justice. In this case the liberty of the press is not merely a guarantee, but it is the only guarantee, of their liberty and their security which the citizens possess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rulers propose to abolish press independence, the people may reasonably demand: 'Give us the right of prosecuting your offences before the ordinary tribunals, and perhaps we may then waive our right of appeal to the tribunal of public opinion.' Use of the press as a public accountability mechanism is justified where judicial remedies are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press correlative to popular sovereignty; censorship absurd under universal suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: When the right of every citizen to co-operate in the government of society is acknowledged, every citizen must be presumed to possess the power of discriminating between the different opinions of his contemporaries ... The sovereignty of the people and the liberty of the press may therefore be looked upon as correlative institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In polities that accept popular participation, restricting the press contradicts the presumption that citizens can judge for themselves; censorship and universal suffrage are 'irreconcilably opposed.' Policy-makers should treat press liberty as integral to the functioning of popular sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial prosecutions of journalists are counterproductive and publicize ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: If you proceed, you must bring the delinquent before a court of permanent judges. But even here the cause must be heard before it can be decided; and the very principles which no book would have ventured to avow are blazoned forth in the pleadings, and what was obscurely hinted at in a single composition is then repeated in a multitude of other publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing alleged press offenders to trial can spread and amplify the criticized opinions; jury acquittal converts a single individual's opinion into broader public opinion. Enforcement via public courts risks magnifying the abusive expression rather than suppressing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship alone insufficient — suppression of press tends toward despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: If you establish a censorship of the press, the tongue of the public speaker will still make itself heard, and you have only increased the mischief ... you have been led from the extreme of independence to the extreme of subjection without meeting with a single tenable position for shelter or repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressing printed expression without addressing other channels of speech (public oratory, assemblies) will not eliminate the spread of opinions and may concentrate power in a way that produces despotism. Regulators should consider the broader speech ecosystem before imposing censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press is simultaneously indispensable to freedom and nearly incompatible with public order
rubrics_metrics.description: It constitutes a singular power, so strangely composed of mingled good and evil that it is at the same time indispensable to the existence of freedom, and nearly incompatible with the maintenance of public order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers must accept trade-offs: to enjoy the inestimable benefits of press freedom, a society must tolerate certain inevitable evils (disorder, abuse). Expecting freedom's benefits without its costs is an illusion that can mislead nations in crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication and decentralization of press reduces individual journal influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of periodical and occasional publications which appears in the United States actually surpasses belief ... the only way to neutralize the effect of public journals is to multiply them indefinitely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural factors — many small papers, absence of a centralized metropolis, low barriers to entry (no licenses, securities, or stamp duties) — diffuse influence among many organs, preventing any single journal from forming overwhelming currents of opinion. Increasing diversity of outlets can be a deliberate strategy to limit press power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic composition of newspapers affects political content (ads reduce political space)
rubrics_metrics.description: In America three-quarters of the enormous sheet which is set before the reader are filled with advertisements, and the remainder is frequently occupied by political intelligence or trivial anecdotes: it is only from time to time that one finds a corner devoted to passionate discussions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The financial model of newspapers (heavy advertising, low returns) leads to less sustained political argument and often lower-quality journalism; this affects the press's role in shaping deep political passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical character/style of journalists matters — American press appeals coarsely to passions
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristics of the American journalist consist in an open and coarse appeal to the passions of the populace; and he habitually abandons the principles of political science to assail the characters of individuals, to track them into private life, and disclose all their weaknesses and errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate journalistic practices for tone and methods: coarse personal attacks and sensationalism are flagged as abuses of intellectual power that degrade public discourse and civic morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press leads to tenacity and durability of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The nations amongst which this liberty exists are as apt to cling to their opinions from pride as from conviction. They cherish them because they hold them to be just, and because they exercised their own free-will in choosing them; and they maintain them not only because they are true, but because they are their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free expression can produce more deeply rooted and long-lasting public convictions (for better or worse). Expect durable public beliefs and resistance to change where public debate is free and participatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press amplifies and reshapes intuitive convictions, sometimes provoking sudden revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the liberty of the press acts upon men who are in the first of these three states [implicit belief without inquiry], it does not immediately disturb their habit of believing implicitly without investigation, but it constantly modifies the objects of their intuitive convictions ... Such are the symptoms of sudden revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the differential effects of press discourse on audiences in different epistemic states: those inclined to accept assertions without inquiry are especially susceptible to sudden shifts when targeted by passionate press campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three degrees of political association (societies, meetings, electoral representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An association consists simply in the public assent which a number of individuals give to certain doctrines ... The second degree is the power of meeting ... Lastly ... they may unite in electoral bodies, and choose delegates to represent them in a central assembly. This is, properly speaking, the application of the representative system to a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess associations by their degree of organization and power: (1) intellectual societies that promote doctrines, (2) localized centers/meetings that coordinate action, (3) electoral delegations that act like a 'government within the government' and can draft or attack laws. Each degree entails greater authority and greater potential impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unrestrained liberty of political association is more dangerous than liberty of the press but may be necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The unrestrained liberty of association cannot be entirely assimilated to the liberty of the press. The one is at the same time less necessary and more dangerous than the other. A nation may confine it within certain limits without forfeiting any part of its self-control; and it may sometimes be obliged to do so in order to maintain its own authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should treat association differently from press: limits on associations may be defensible to preserve state authority while retaining overall liberty. Evaluate need for restrictions carefully, balancing dangers against their utility as checks on majority power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations as necessary substitutes/checks against majority despotism in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no countries in which associations are more needed, to prevent the despotism of faction or the arbitrary power of a prince, than those which are democratically constituted ... In countries in which these associations do not exist, if private individuals are unable to create an artificial and a temporary substitute for them, I can imagine no permanent protection against the most galling tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In democracies lacking aristocratic counterbalances, encourage voluntary associations as institutional checks on the majority and as means to organize minority interests; though potentially dangerous, they can protect pluralism and prevent concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large political conventions can assume legislative character and threaten public tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in a people which is imperfectly accustomed to the exercise of freedom, or which is exposed to violent political passions, a deliberating minority, which confines itself to the contemplation of future laws, be placed in juxtaposition to the legislative majority, I cannot but believe that public tranquillity incurs very great risks ... their debates at Philadelphia ... at once assumed a legislative character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor mass political gatherings and conventions for tendencies to go beyond consultation into quasi-legislative action; such transitions raise risks of destabilization and may precipitate extralegal political movements (example: tariff Convention of 1831 influencing revolt in 1832).

rubrics_metrics.name: Free associations reduce secret conspiracies but multiply factions
rubrics_metrics.description: In countries where associations are free, secret societies are unknown. In America there are numerous factions, but no conspiracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust associational sphere encourages open factionalism rather than secret plotting; this openness can be a stabilizing feature, even if it increases visible political strife. Policy that channels dissent into lawful associations can lower risk of conspiratorial violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations can be perverted or carried to excess; require discretion in management
rubrics_metrics.description: If the liberty of association is a fruitful source of advantages and prosperity to some nations, it may be perverted or carried to excess by others, and the element of life may be changed into an element of destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulate or guide associations where necessary to prevent excesses: evaluate their purposes, means, and impacts. Comparative study of well-managed vs. degenerate associations can inform prudent limits and norms.
